newsitem.title: USA: Gore, Kemp expect civilized debate of issues.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Kemp expect civilized debate of issues.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

Vice President Al Gore and Republican Jack Kemp say they want a civilised, issues-oriented campaign debate on Wednesday evening, when both will be on display as possible presidential candidates for the year 2000.

"I do not see this as a boxing match," Kemp, who is Bob Dole's running-mate, told the St Petersburg Times. "I see it as an opportunity to discuss family matters with the American people and our national family through television."
Gore said he would try to echo the themes of Democratic President Bill Clinton, who leads Dole in the polls less than four weeks before Nov. 5 Election Day.
He said in his own interview with the St. Petersburg Times that he respected Kemp's positive approach and predicted it would be "possible to disagree without being disagreeable."
"He has resisted the advice from some in their party to make harsh attacks on the president and me, and I admire that," Gore said.

Dole and Clinton also had a relatively gentlemanly encounter in the first of their two campaign debates on Sunday, but some Republicans complained Dole had gone too easy on the president and he has begun hitting Clinton harder.

He drew a White House rebuke on Tuesday after he made a flippant reference to Clinton as "Bozo," pointedly dodged a reporter's question about the president's personal ethics and said at one rally, "My word is good, his word is no good."

The 90-minute Gore-Kemp encounter at the Mehaffey Centre, in this resort and retirement haven on the Gulf of Mexico, is the fifth vice presidential debate to be held since Dole, then running mate on President Gerald Ford's losing re-election ticket, met Democrat Walter Mondale in the first one in 1976.
Previous debates had little or no effect on presidential elections, although they have occasionally had great influence on the careers of those who took part.
In 1988, Democrat Lloyd Bentsen crushed Republican Dan Quayle with the withering retort, "Senator, you're no Jack Kennedy," when the young and inexperienced Quayle had drawn that comparison.
The celebrated zinger did not harm Republican nominee George Bush, who routed Democrat Michael Dukakis in the election, but it has stuck to Quayle ever since.
And Dole himself has been trying to shake off a reputation for meanness solidified in the public's mind by his bitter, attack-dog style in that long-ago debate with Mondale.

This year, neither Gore nor Kemp need to prove their vice presidential qualifications. A Gallup poll this week found 76 percent of voters thought Gore was qualified to be president. Kemp, who is not quiite as well known, scored 61 percent.
That makes the stakes especially high, since both have presidential ambitions for the year 2000 and both are seen as early frontrunners for their party nominations.

"This debate sure looks like it could be a preview, although four years is an awfully long time in politics. But that aspect could colour the way they debate," said Richard Scher, a political scientist at the University of Florida.
"They will obviously use this opportunity to position themselves for the future and try to act presidential."

Kemp has made his vice presidential campaign into a crusade to widen the appeal of the Republican Party. He has gone into inner cities and black ghettos where few Republicans have bothered to campaign before.
"Our party has to do a lot more to reach out to blacks and Latinos and immigrants and women and young people," he said.

Gore has played the more traditional running mate role of energising the Democratic party base. He has also worked hard to loosen up, fighting an image for being dull and wooden by starting each speech with a string of self-deprecating jokes.
He strategically cast himself as the underdog ahead of the showdown, calling Kemp "a past master" at the art of debate.
